text: The last three lessons moved a model from research artifact to a packaged, served, lineage-tracked production system. This lesson turns the arrow back around: once a model is live, what it encounters in production — drift, failure cases, edge cases nobody trained for — is real signal for the next research cycle, not just an operations concern handled separately.

The loop closes in stages. Production logs predictions and confidence as the raw material. Drift and low-confidence cases get flagged as a statistical signal, not a vague feeling that something's off. Those hard examples get reviewed periodically and folded into the next eval set. And a sustained signal — not a single noisy alert — is what actually triggers a new research cycle.

The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares a feature's distribution in a recent production window against its distribution in training, producing a p-value for whether they're statistically distinguishable. Run per-feature on a schedule against a rolling window, and 'the model feels off lately' becomes a quantified signal: which feature moved, and how confidently.

Drift detection catches distribution shift, not individual hard cases. So separately, log any prediction with low confidence, or one a user explicitly flagged as wrong, into a growing hard-examples set. The research team reviews a sample periodically and folds the genuinely hard, representative ones into the next training run's eval set — which is how a model's blind spots get found by the people equipped to fix them.

That closes Chapter 8, and with it, the course's main chapters — reading papers, structuring codebases, scaling experiments, debugging, collaborating, and now shipping a model while keeping the loop back to research closed. What's left is the capstone: Chapter 9, where you reproduce a real published result and extend it, starting with Lesson 42's paper selection.
